author: Carlos Martinez
title: HOTAS and Button Panels for Sim Racing: Setup and Real Trade-offs
description: Learn how to mount HOTAS sticks and button panels on a racing rig, what they're actually useful for, and how to avoid wasting money on gear that sits unused.

sections.p: A HOTAS (hands-on throttle-and-stick) setup and a full button panel look impressive in a racing cockpit. They promise precision control, immersion, and the kind of hardware you see in professional esports streams. The reality is more mixed. Most sim racers never need them, many who buy them use them poorly, and a few find they unlock genuine advantages in specific cars and series. This guide cuts through the marketing to show you what these controls actually do, when they matter, and how to integrate them without breaking your budget or workflow.

sections.h2: What HOTAS and button panels actually do

sections.p: A HOTAS stick (or pair of sticks) gives you analog input on two axes independent of your steering wheel. In sim racing, that typically means pitch (nose up/down) and roll (wings left/right) in aircraft-like cars, or adjustable input for trim, differential, brake bias, and fuel mix in road and oval cars. A button panel is a collection of buttons, toggles, rotary dials, and switches mounted near your wheel or on an armrest, all programmable to any in-game function. Neither is essential. Both require time to set up, cable management, and mental bandwidth during a race to remember what each button does.

The appeal is real but specific. In open-cockpit formula cars, a HOTAS stick can feel more natural than the wheel for adjustments that happen mid-corner. In endurance racing, button panels reduce the number of times you have to move your hands off the wheel to adjust fuel, tire balance, or pit-stop strategy. In rally and dirt racing, some drivers map handbrake and clutch to analog axes for finer control than a binary button press. But in a 30-minute sprint race with no adjustments, or on a track where setup is locked in, neither does anything.

HOTAS sticks shine in cars that allow mid-race adjustments and reward quick, smooth inputs. Formula cars with adjustable front and rear wings, differential stiffness, or brake bias are the clearest case. The stick feels fast once mapped correctly, and your hands never leave the wheel. Prototype racing (LMP2, GTP) is similar. You are adjusting fuel, brake bias, engine braking, and hybrid power output throughout a stint, and buttons feel slow if you do dozens of adjustments per race.

In GT3 racing, the case is weaker. Many endurance GT events lock setup at the start of a race. Some allow fuel and tire balance adjustment. If you are in a team with one driver per stint and no in-race changes allowed, a HOTAS adds no value. If you are in a long-distance solo event with 4+ hours of driving, the speed of a stick for fuel and balance adjustments could save you seconds per pit window. That trades off against the complexity of learning the mapping during a race when focus is already divided.

Oval racing is a gray area. You rarely adjust anything mid-race in stock cars. Single-seaters sometimes allow adjustments between laps or cautions. Unless you are chasing iRating at a high level in a series that explicitly rewards quick adjustments, oval drivers can skip HOTAS entirely.

Button panels are more universal than HOTAS sticks because they can be mapped to anything. Pit brake, lights, gear change, fuel mixture, differential, tire adjustment, radio, spotter on/off, replay capture, chat. The panel itself is just an interface. What matters is whether you use it faster than the wheel's native controls.

list: Buttons work best for binary functions (on/off, increment/decrement) where you do the same action repeatedly in a race. Pit brake, lights, and gear change in sequential manual cars are classic examples.
Rotary dials and encoders are slower than buttons for quick adjustments but faster than a steering-wheel menu if you need smooth, gradual input like fuel or brake-bias trim.
Buttons take mental load. In a league race, you are managing racing line, tire temperature, fuel load, and other drivers. If you have to remember which button is which, you lose focus.
Ergonomic placement matters enormously. A button in easy reach of your thumb is usable. A button that requires you to move your hand or glance down is dangerous and usually abandoned in a real race.

sections.p: HOTAS sticks mount on either side of your seat, usually clamped to the same rig structure as your cockpit frame. They should be close enough to your body that you can reach them without moving your seat forward or leaning sideways. If they are too far away, you will not use them. If they are mounted too low or at an awkward angle, your wrist and forearm will fatigue faster than your hands on the wheel.

Button panels bolt to the rig as well. Common positions are on a small platform in front of your lap (like a mini shifter stand), on an armrest extension, or on a vertical panel to the left of the wheel where your elbow rests. The best location depends on your cockpit geometry and what you are mapping. Pit-brake buttons go where your thumb naturally lives when braking hard. Fuel adjustment goes somewhere you can reach without thinking.

Cable routing becomes critical once you have HOTAS, pedals, wheel, and a button panel all connected. Use cable ties, conduit, and a powered USB hub to keep things organized and reduce the risk of a yanked cable during a race crash. If your PC loses connection to your controller during a race, you will cut out of the session looking like a disconnect. Test all cable paths under load before racing.

HOTAS sticks range from ~150 to ~400 USD depending on resolution, haptic feedback, and brand. Button panels range from ~100 (a simple 12-button box) to ~500 (a full rally-style switchboard with encoders, toggles, and LEDs). The cheapest entry is a single HOTAS stick plus a small button panel, around ~250 total. A full professional setup (dual HOTAS, large panel, mounting hardware) can exceed ~800.

list: Start with a single HOTAS stick if you race formula or prototype regularly, not both sticks immediately. One stick handles pitch and roll in most sims.
Buy a button panel only after you have identified 4+ functions you will actually use in every race session. If you are thinking ahead to future games or series you have not raced yet, skip it.
Verify compatibility with your rig's mounting system before buying. Most HOTAS sticks use standard clamps, but cockpit frames vary in depth, angle, and bolt patterns.
Check that the stick and buttons support whatever control mapping your sim and wheel base allow. Some wheels have limited button mapping; some do not support axis input from external devices.
Test the stick and buttons in a practice session, not a race, until you are confident. Retraining muscle memory mid-season is a quick way to ruin your iRating.

sections.p: Many drivers buy a HOTAS or button panel because they look cool on stream and then rarely use them. The setup cost (physical mounting, cable routing, button mapping, muscle memory) is higher than beginners expect. If you are in your first season or driving three different series, do not add this complexity yet.

Mapping too many functions to your panel guarantees that you will forget what half of them do. Under pressure in a race, you will reach for the wrong button, overshoot an adjustment, or cause a pit-road penalty because you hit the pit-limiter instead of pit-brake. Map only the functions you will touch at least once per race, and place them where your muscle memory naturally goes.

Mounting HOTAS or button panels in inconvenient locations (too far away, too low, requiring a glance to find them) almost always leads to them sitting unused. A perfectly functional stick that you can only reach by leaning is worse than no stick at all, because you waste cockpit space and cable clutter.

sections.tip: If you race in a league with consistent series, cars, and pit-stop rules, a small button panel mapped to that specific series can pay for itself in time saved and mistakes avoided. If you switch series every season, the return on investment drops significantly.

sections.h2: Practical integration with a typical rig

sections.p: On a single-monitor setup like the one used at RealIRacing, visual clutter and reach distance are constraints. HOTAS sticks mounted on a standard cockpit frame will not interfere with steering or pedals if clamped to the seat frame. A button panel can sit on a small platform between your pedals and wheel base, but it has to be low enough that your hands can find it at speed without looking down.

Cable management is the unglamorous reality. Each stick has a USB or USB-C cable running to your PC or a powered hub. Each button panel needs power and data. If you are streaming your races with OBS, you are already managing wheel, pedals, shifter or handbrake, monitor, and camera gear. HOTAS and panels add more USB connections and more cables to route around your cockpit frame and monitor stand.

Test your button mapping in practice mode before racing. Load a car you use the sticks for, go to a test track, and spend 10 minutes hitting every button and moving every stick axis to confirm that the input registers in-game and that you can reach it comfortably at speed. A button that works in the garage but is unreachable during a hard-braking zone is a hazard, not a tool.

sections.h2: The real question: do you need this?

sections.p: If you are racing GT3 endurance events with long stints and mid-race fuel and balance adjustments, a HOTAS stick or small button panel for fuel/brake-bias control will save you time and thought. If you are racing formula or prototype, a HOTAS stick is a reasonable investment. If you are racing oval stock cars or doing short sprints where setup is locked, skip both. If you are under 3000 iRating and still learning racecraft and consistency, focus on the wheel, pedals, and monitor quality first. HOTAS and button panels amplify the skill of a fast driver but do not create it.

faqs.q: Can I use HOTAS sticks for steering input instead of a wheel?
faqs.a: Technically yes, most sims allow dual-stick steering (pitch and roll mapped to steering and throttle/brake). In practice, almost no one does this in road racing. Dual sticks feel unintuitive after a steering wheel and reduce your ability to make fine corrections. Some rally drivers use dual sticks for the analog control, but road racing cars expect wheel input.

faqs.q: How many buttons do I actually need on a panel?
faqs.a: Start with 6 to 8 buttons mapped to functions you use every race. Pit brake, lights, and fuel or brake balance are common. A panel with 24 buttons where you use 4 of them wastes space and mental load. Build the panel as you identify functions that you reach for constantly and get frustrated having to menu-dive for.

faqs.q: Do HOTAS sticks work with all wheelbase brands?
faqs.a: HOTAS sticks connect via USB or USB-C, independent of your wheel base. The wheel base brand does not matter. What matters is that your sim (iRacing, ACC, etc.) and your wheel base firmware support axis mapping from external devices. Check your wheel base documentation and the sim's controller settings before buying a stick.

faqs.q: Is a button panel useful for oval racing?
faqs.a: Less so than road racing. Stock cars rarely allow mid-race setup changes, so fuel adjustment and brake bias are locked in. A button panel makes sense only if your series allows caution-flag adjustments or if you want to map pit commands and lights. For pure sprint oval racing, a panel adds complexity without much return.
